original.title: Hiring: criteria before candidates
original.summary: To help you run a selection you can explain to anyone who asks.
original.whyItMatters: Legal facts as of October 2026. Check with Human Resources for changes, including any ruling in United States v. Minnesota.
body: Remember. Decide on job-related criteria set before you see candidates. Do not weigh race, sex, disability or any other protected trait in an individual selection. Reach widely. Keep every door open to anyone. Same answer to pressure in any direction. Write what is true, and keep it.

Before posting. Ask Human Resources about the required order: under MAPE Article 16, posting, interest bids, layoff lists, claims, then other means. Check other agreements. Get the position description. Write four to six criteria from the duties, with anchors. Date them. Test each requirement: who does it exclude, and does the job need it? State language needs as skills. State cultural competence as behaviors. Do not use cultural intelligence, IDI or results from this app. Ask how justification works today.

Reaching people. Share widely, including disability and community networks and greater Minnesota. Keep events and messages open to anyone. Include the accommodation notice. Forward any request promptly. Give the same information to everyone.

The interview. Same questions, same order, same time. Neutral follow-ups. Nothing about health, family, faith, national origin or age. Arrange access early. Score the answer, not the delivery. Score independently first. Then discuss. When someone says "fit": "Which criterion? What did they say?"

The decision. Compare side by side, and write a reason tied to the criteria. If directed to weigh a trait: decide on criteria, ask for any written basis, and report to Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer. If justification is required: write the truth, from your dated records. Keep criteria, scores and reasons unchanged. Ask about retention and preservation.
Do next. Call Human Resources before your next vacancy opens, and ask what they already provide.

Provide any required justification from accurate, dated records. Preserve the original criteria, scores and reasons; document corrections transparently rather than rewriting the record to defend a result. Follow applicable retention and preservation requirements.

original.title: What a Supervisor Should Know About the Rules, Fall 2026: job aid
original.summary: A one-page reminder of what binds you, what is an enforcement position, and what to do while the rules move. Dated October 2026. Check before relying on it.
body: Remember. General information, not legal advice. This app is voluntary and does not satisfy Minn. Stat. 43A.21. The state's own training does. "Reported" means the source was secondary. Verify it before you repeat it as fact.

Binding on you now. Immediately report harassment and discrimination concerns to Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer (Policies 1436 and 1329). Promptly forward accommodation requests and tell the person who decides. Never ask for medical information (Policy 1433). One Title VII standard for all employees (Ames). "Some harm" is enough (Muldrow). The Human Rights Act covers harassment under "discriminate" (2024 c. 105). Complete the state's required training (43A.21, Supervisor Core or Manager Core). Ask Human Resources what applies.

Enforcement positions to know. EEOC technical assistance, March 19, 2025: training, mentoring and access can be terms of employment. No identity-sorted programs. Client preference is no defense to race or color discrimination. DOJ guidance, July 29, 2025: non-binding, with practical force through OMB M-25-33. No required affirmation or confession. No penalties for dissent. Federal agencies have stepped back from disparate impact and an integration mandate. Courts, states and private plaintiffs are not bound by those opinions.

Say it this way. Disparate impact: "Federal enforcement has largely moved away from it. The Title VII provision and Minnesota law still exist. We use data to review our process, not to decide about an individual." Olmstead: "The decision and the statutes remain. The federal enforcement position has changed. Minnesota's commitments continue." United States v. Minnesota: "It is pending. No court has ruled. I will share what Human Resources tells me."

Dates to hold. April 26, 2027: DOJ Title II web rule, entities of 50,000 or more. May 11, 2027: HHS Section 504 web rule, recipients with 15 or more employees (reported). March 1, 2027 and July 15, 2027: discovery and dispositive motion dates in United States v. Minnesota (reported). Accessibility under state standards applies now.

Do next. Write your reason before your next assignment, schedule change or hire. Save your Human Resources, Affirmative Action Officer, ADA coordinator and labor relations contacts. Set calendar reminders to ask what has changed in January, April and July 2027.

changes.after: Apply current policy. Under Policies 1436 and 1329, managers and supervisors must immediately report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination, including sexual harassment, to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Promptly forward accommodation requests and tell the requester who will decide. Under Policy 1433, supervisors must not request medical information from someone seeking an accommodation; the ADA coordinator handles any appropriate documentation request. Complete assigned state training. Ames rejects a heightened evidentiary burden for majority-group Title VII claimants. Muldrow concerns discriminatory job transfers: harm to an employment term or condition need not be significant. These holdings do not replace review of the facts and applicable requirements.

changes.before: Enforcement positions to know. EEOC technical assistance, March 19, 2025: training, mentoring and access can be terms of employment. No identity-sorted programs. Client preference is no defense to race or color discrimination. DOJ guidance, July 29, 2025: non-binding, with practical force through OMB M-25-33. No required affirmation or confession. No penalties for dissent. Federal agencies have stepped back from disparate impact and an integration mandate. Courts, states and private plaintiffs are not bound by those opinions.
changes.after: Understand enforcement guidance. The EEOC’s March 2025 technical assistance addresses discrimination in hiring, training, mentoring and other employment opportunities. The DOJ’s July 29, 2025 funding-recipient guidance identifies non-binding best practices; OMB M-25-33 directs federal agencies to follow that guidance in administering federal programs. Distinguish those agency positions from statutes and court rulings. Have the responsible legal or Human Resources office review program-specific implications, including participation criteria and retaliation protections, rather than treating a course summary as a legal determination.

Minnesota, obtain the current case status and any operative orders through Human Resources or legal counsel. original.title: Why Equity Is a Supervisor's Work: job aid
original.summary: A one-page reminder of why this is a supervisor's work, what evidence supports, and what to do next.
body: Remember. Training teaches. Your decisions decide. Apart from the Equity Analysis Toolkit, which is required of all DHS staff, this app is voluntary. It keeps no scores, sends nothing to your supervisor or employer, and does not satisfy Minn. Stat. 43A.21. Nothing here promises to reduce disparities. Check what happens in your own unit.

What the evidence supports. Knowledge and near-term attitudes can move. Lasting behavior and outcomes are harder. Awareness alone has a poor record. Better support: structured decisions, visible criteria, named responsibility, and feedback from your own team. Mandatory versus voluntary is unsettled. Formal tools can backfire without review.

Where equity gets decided. Who gets your time. Who gets visible and routine work. What you write, and what follows from a rating. How you hire. How fast you move requests and reports. Whether everyone can take part in the meeting.
Four habits. Write the criteria first. Keep a simple record. Ask your team the same questions, about the work. Look at the result and change the process.
Watch for. "We handle that here" after a course or a program. An average that hides who was harmed. Paperwork filled in after you have decided. Asking one person to speak for a group.
Do next. Write your four lines: decision, tool, date, check. Use the tool once this week. Look at it again in 90 days.

changes.before: Remember. Training teaches. Your decisions decide. Apart from the Equity Analysis Toolkit, which is required of all DHS staff, this app is voluntary. It keeps no scores, sends nothing to your supervisor or employer, and does not satisfy Minn. Stat. 43A.21. Nothing here promises to reduce disparities. Check what happens in your own unit.
changes.after: Remember. Learning can inform a decision, but completion alone does not show that practice or outcomes improved. This program does not offer training credits. Optional learning supports DHS responsibilities under the Equity Policy, including applicable equity-analysis requirements and assigned agency training. Complete required training through the agency’s designated process. Follow the privacy notice for the feature you use, and keep confidential personnel or case information in authorized work systems.
changes.reason: Use accepted program-credit distinction and remove unsupported whole-app no-score/no-transmission promises.

changes.before: What the evidence supports. Knowledge and near-term attitudes can move. Lasting behavior and outcomes are harder. Awareness alone has a poor record. Better support: structured decisions, visible criteria, named responsibility, and feedback from your own team. Mandatory versus voluntary is unsettled. Formal tools can backfire without review.
changes.after: What the evidence supports. Bezrukova and colleagues’ 2016 meta-analysis found stronger effects on knowledge and training reactions than on attitudes or behavior, with results varying by design and context. Chang and colleagues’ 2019 trial at one organization found different attitude and behavior effects across groups. Neither establishes that completing a course improves outcomes in a particular DHS unit. Use clear criteria, accountable decisions and feedback, then examine what actually happens rather than assuming a tool or training is effective.
changes.reason: Primary research abstracts opened; distinguish heterogeneous findings from categorical ineffectiveness and do not assert all specific organizational practices proved by these two studies.

changes.before: Where equity gets decided. Who gets your time. Who gets visible and routine work. What you write, and what follows from a rating. How you hire. How fast you move requests and reports. Whether everyone can take part in the meeting.
changes.after: Where supervisors influence equity. Examine access to your time and support; the distribution of visible and routine work; the evidence used in ratings and hiring; how requests and reports are handled; and whether staff can participate in meetings. Identify which decisions you control and which require another role or process.
changes.reason: Develop fragments into usable scope without enlarging supervisor authority.

changes.before: Four habits. Write the criteria first. Keep a simple record. Ask your team the same questions, about the work. Look at the result and change the process.
changes.after: Four habits. Establish relevant criteria before deciding. Keep required records in the appropriate system. Invite feedback through consistent, accessible questions about the work. Review the evidence and decide whether to retain a sound practice, address a barrier or seek further review.
changes.reason: Avoid forced change, informal records and identical-method barriers.

changes.before: Watch for. "We handle that here" after a course or a program. An average that hides who was harmed. Paperwork filled in after you have decided. Asking one person to speak for a group.
changes.after: Watch for unsupported conclusions. A completed course does not prove that a concern has been addressed. An average can conceal different experiences. Records written after a decision may miss how it was reached. One person’s account should be heard without treating that person as a representative of an entire group.
changes.reason: Replace slogans with the reasoning they are meant to teach.

changes.before: Do next. Write your four lines: decision, tool, date, check. Use the tool once this week. Look at it again in 90 days.
changes.after: Do next. Choose a decision or practice within your role. Identify the evidence, the responsible people, any required process and when its effects should be reviewed. If you use a fictional example for optional learning, keep it separate from official records. For real work, follow applicable duties and review timing rather than treating a fixed practice interval as a requirement.
changes.reason: Separate optional learning from work duties and remove arbitrary one-week/90-day instructions.
